name: William Tyndale

died.cause: Executed: strangled and burned as a heretic

summary: English scholar who made the first printed New Testament in English, translated directly from the Greek, and whose wording carried through into the King James Bible; he was executed for heresy in 1536.

key_dates.label: Tutor in the Walsh household at Little Sodbury, Gloucestershire
Asks Bishop Cuthbert Tunstall of London to support a translation and is turned down
Leaves England for Germany to translate in exile
First printing at Cologne is raided; he escapes with part of the sheets
Complete English New Testament printed at Worms
Publishes The Obedience of a Christian Man
Publishes the Pentateuch, translated from Hebrew
Publishes his revised New Testament at Antwerp
Betrayed by Henry Phillips; arrested in Antwerp and imprisoned at Vilvoorde

accomplishments.text: Translated the New Testament into English directly from the Greek. It was the first New Testament printed in English (Worms, 1526); earlier Wycliffite versions were hand-copied translations from the Latin Vulgate.

Aimed to put Scripture in the hands of ordinary people. Foxe reports him telling a learned opponent that, if God spared his life, he would cause "a boy that driveth the plough" to know more of the Scripture than he did.

Worked in exile after failing to get a bishop's backing in England. His New Testaments were smuggled into England, where church authorities bought up and burned copies, including a public burning at St Paul's in 1526.
Translated the first five books of the Old Testament (1530) and Jonah (1531) from Hebrew, the first English translations of those books made from the Hebrew.
Wrote The Obedience of a Christian Man (1528), arguing for the authority of Scripture and for the obedience of subjects to their king rather than to the pope.
Opposed Henry VIII's plan to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon in The Practice of Prelates (1530), costing himself the king's favor.
Defended his translation choices and Reformation teaching in a printed debate with Sir Thomas More, including An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue (1531).
Introduced English words such as "Passover" and "scapegoat," along with many phrases still in common use (see Words and sayings below).

Laid the foundation of later English Bibles: his work was the basis of Matthew's Bible (1537) and the Great Bible (1539). One study estimates that about 83% of the King James New Testament (1611) keeps his wording.
Was condemned as a heretic and executed at Vilvoorde in 1536. Foxe records his last words as a prayer: "Lord, open the King of England's eyes."

sayings_intro: A selection of well-attested examples, not a complete list. Most reached modern English through the King James Bible (1611), which kept much of Tyndale's wording. "Original" is based on the earliest recorded use in the Oxford English Dictionary, or on comparison with the earlier Wycliffite Bible (translated from Latin in the late 1300s), which worded the same verse differently. New Testament verses are from his 1526/1534 translation; Old Testament verses are from his 1530 Pentateuch.

original.note: Coined from "pass over" to render the Hebrew pesach; earlier English writers mostly used the borrowed word "pasch."

persecution_note: Tyndale spent his last eleven years as a fugitive. He was hunted by English church and royal authorities, betrayed in Antwerp, tried for heresy under the Holy Roman Emperor's laws, and executed in 1536. People who read or distributed his books in England were also arrested, and several were burned.

persecution.title: Accused of heresy before the diocesan chancellor
persecution.summary: While Tyndale was tutor at Little Sodbury, local clergy who objected to his views reported him. He was called before the chancellor of the Diocese of Worcester, who, by the account Foxe preserves, threatened and abused him. No formal charge followed.

responsible.name: John Bell
responsible.role: Chancellor of the Diocese of Worcester (later Bishop of Worcester)
responsible.jurisdiction: Diocese of Worcester, English Church (then under papal authority)

responsible.name: Local Gloucestershire clergy
responsible.role: Reported him to the diocese

persecution.outcome: Released with a warning. He left for London soon afterward.

persecution.title: Printing of his New Testament stopped at Cologne
persecution.summary: The Catholic controversialist Johann Cochlaeus learned that an English New Testament was being printed in Cologne. He alerted the city authorities through the senator Hermann Rinck, and the city council banned the printing.

responsible.name: Johann Cochlaeus
responsible.role: Catholic theologian and anti-Lutheran writer; informed the authorities

responsible.name: Hermann Rinck
responsible.role: Cologne city senator; obtained the ban
responsible.jurisdiction: Free Imperial City of Cologne, Holy Roman Empire

responsible.name: City council of Cologne
responsible.role: Prohibited the printing
responsible.jurisdiction: Free Imperial City of Cologne, Holy Roman Empire

persecution.outcome: Tyndale and his assistant William Roye fled up the Rhine to Worms with the sheets already printed, and completed the New Testament there in 1526.

persecution.title: His New Testament banned and burned in England
persecution.summary: When copies reached England, the Bishop of London banned the translation and preached against it at St Paul's Cross, where copies were burned in October 1526. The Archbishop of Canterbury arranged for copies to be bought up abroad so they could be destroyed. In 1530 a royal proclamation, issued after a meeting of bishops and scholars, banned Tyndale's New Testament and his other books.

responsible.name: Cuthbert Tunstall
responsible.role: Bishop of London; banned the translation and had copies burned
responsible.jurisdiction: Diocese of London, English Church (under papal authority)

responsible.name: William Warham
responsible.role: Archbishop of Canterbury; organized buying up copies to destroy them

responsible.name: Cardinal Thomas Wolsey
responsible.role: Lord Chancellor and papal legate; led the 1526 campaign against Lutheran books in England

responsible.name: Henry VIII
responsible.role: King of England; issued the 1530 proclamation banning the books

persecution.outcome: Most copies of the 1526 edition were destroyed. Only three copies are known to survive.

persecution.title: Arrest and burning of his readers and distributors in England
persecution.summary: As Lord Chancellor, Sir Thomas More wrote at length against Tyndale and pursued people who owned or smuggled his books. Several were burned as heretics, among them Thomas Hitton (1530), Richard Bayfield (1531), and James Bainham (1532). Tyndale's brother John was fined in 1530 and paraded through London with the books he had distributed pinned to his clothing.

responsible.name: Sir Thomas More
responsible.role: Lord Chancellor of England (1529–1532); interrogated suspects and wrote against Tyndale

responsible.name: John Stokesley
responsible.role: Bishop of London from 1530; tried heresy suspects, including Bayfield and Bainham

responsible.name: William Warham
responsible.role: Archbishop of Canterbury; condemned Thomas Hitton

persecution.outcome: Several of Tyndale's readers and smugglers were executed, and many more were made to recant. Tyndale himself was out of reach on the Continent.

persecution.title: Henry VIII seeks his return
persecution.summary: Henry VIII was angered by The Practice of Prelates, which opposed the annulment of his marriage. He had his agent Stephen Vaughan try to persuade Tyndale to come back to England. When Tyndale refused, the king sought to have him handed over from the emperor's lands, according to Daniell through his ambassador Sir Thomas Elyot.

responsible.name: Henry VIII
responsible.role: King of England; wanted Tyndale returned

responsible.name: Sir Thomas Elyot
responsible.role: English ambassador to Charles V

persecution.outcome: Tyndale stayed in Antwerp, protected by the English merchants' house there.

persecution.title: Betrayed and arrested in Antwerp
persecution.summary: Henry Phillips, a young Englishman who had won Tyndale's trust, lured him out of the English House in Antwerp, where he was protected, and pointed him out to imperial officers waiting outside. Tyndale was taken to the state prison in the castle of Vilvoorde, near Brussels. Who paid Phillips is unknown. Historians have suspected English conservative clergy, including Bishop John Stokesley of London, but this has not been proven.

responsible.name: Henry Phillips
responsible.role: Befriended and betrayed him

responsible.name: Pierre Dufief
responsible.role: Procurator-general (chief prosecutor); led the arrest

responsible.name: Government of the Habsburg Netherlands
responsible.role: Ordered and held the arrest (regent: Mary of Hungary)
responsible.jurisdiction: Habsburg Netherlands, under Emperor Charles V

defended_by.name: Thomas Poyntz
defended_by.role: English merchant who sheltered him; campaigned for his release and was himself arrested, later escaping

defended_by.name: Thomas Cromwell
defended_by.role: Henry VIII's chief minister; wrote letters seeking his release

persecution.outcome: Imprisoned at Vilvoorde for about sixteen months.

persecution.title: Heresy trial and execution
persecution.summary: Tyndale was tried for heresy under Charles V's edicts against Lutheranism. The commission included theologians from the University of Louvain, who examined him and wrote against his views. He was condemned in August 1536, formally degraded from the priesthood, and handed over to the secular authorities, who strangled him and burned his body at Vilvoorde. No direct part by the pope (Paul III) is recorded: the emperor's government ran the case, with Catholic theologians acting as heresy examiners.

responsible.name: Pierre Dufief
responsible.role: Procurator-general; prosecuted the case

responsible.name: Jacobus Latomus
responsible.role: Louvain theologian; examined him and wrote against his teaching
responsible.jurisdiction: Faculty of Theology, University of Louvain

responsible.name: Ruard Tapper
responsible.role: Louvain theologian; member of the heresy commission
responsible.jurisdiction: Faculty of Theology, University of Louvain

responsible.name: Emperor Charles V's government
responsible.role: Its heresy laws were the basis of the charge; carried out the execution

persecution.outcome: Executed at Vilvoorde, traditionally on 6 October 1536.

excommunication_note: No separate sentence of excommunication against Tyndale by name is recorded before his trial. His condemnation as a heretic in August 1536 cut him off from the Church under canon law, and he was formally degraded from the priesthood before being handed to the secular authorities.

excommunications.by: Heresy commission under Emperor Charles V (with theologians of the University of Louvain)
excommunications.authority: Imperial heresy law in the Habsburg Netherlands; church degradation ceremony at Vilvoorde
excommunications.reason: Condemned as a heretic for his teaching on justification by faith and other Reformation doctrines
excommunications.status: Degraded from the priesthood and executed; never reversed

persecuted_others_note: No record of Tyndale supporting or carrying out persecution of others. He was himself hunted and executed as a heretic; his polemical writings attacked the papacy, the clergy, and Thomas More in harsh terms, but did not call for anyone to be punished.
